statement: The numbers 1 to 9 are written in a 3 by 3 grid, one number in each square. Of the three rows and the three columns, at most how many can have an even sum?

choices.misconception: I assumed the numbers could be arranged so that every row and every column had an even sum.
I saw that the three rows cannot all be even but forgot that the same argument applies to the columns.
I only considered the rows and forgot that the columns count too.
I thought that with five odd numbers to place, at least three of the six lines would have to contain an odd number of odd numbers.

hints: Add up the three row sums. What do you get?
Suppose all three rows had even sums and look for a contradiction with the total of 1 to 9. Then apply the same argument to the columns, and finally check that the bound can actually be reached.
The three row sums add to 1 + 2 + ... + 9 = 45, which is odd, so not all three rows can be even. The same holds for the columns.

solutions.reliable: The three row sums together are 1 + 2 + ... + 9 = 45, which is odd. If all three row sums were even, their total would be even, a contradiction; so at most 2 rows have an even sum. The same argument shows at most 2 columns do. So at most 4 lines are even. This is reached by the grid with rows 1, 3, 2 / 5, 7, 4 / 6, 8, 9: the row sums are 6, 16 and 23, and the column sums are 12, 18 and 15, so two rows and two columns are even. The answer is 4. The transferable idea: assume the best case and show it forces an impossible total, then build an example for the next best case.

whyOnTest: Proof by contradiction shows up as an at most question: assuming the maximum leads to an odd total that cannot be even.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
